title: What Happened to the Software Buyout Boom?
seoTitle: Software Buyouts, 2020–2022: Control and Exit Audit
subtitle: An audit of 25 software take-privates: what changed ownership, what returned cash, and what the public record cannot say about returns.
seoDescription: An August 2026 audit of 25 software take-privates separates control exits, partial liquidity and creditor transfers without treating them as investment returns.

artwork.label: Software buyouts / control, liquidity, and realization
artwork.note: Three separate ledgers: headline transaction value, ownership events, and the control status that determines whether a clean realization occurred.

author: SULAYMAN BOWLES
thesis: Liquidity and a completed control exit answer different questions. The 2020–2022 cohort had ownership changes and cash-generating events, but no clean sponsor realization under the stated definition at the cutoff.

conclusion.title: An unresolved exit is not a measured loss
conclusion.content: No row met the clean-realization test at the cutoff. The control map still records liquidity, restructurings, and ownership changes. Without sponsor cash flows and comparable marks, it cannot establish cohort returns or permanent impairment.

evidenceBoundary: The public package contains a 25-row classification table, claim ledger, methodology note, summary, and fallback web edition. It does not expose the underlying transaction source ledger or sponsor cash flows. The mixed $171.2 billion headline-value total cannot support MOIC, IRR, impairment, or transaction-by-transaction independent verification from this site alone.
content: None of the 25 large sponsor-led software take-privates announced from 2020 through 2022 met this study’s control-based clean-realization test at the August 17, 2026 cutoff. That does not mean every investment lost money. IPOs, stake sales, and refinancings can generate liquidity while the original sponsor group still controls the company.

Company-reported headline values sum to $171.2 billion. The announcements mix valuation definitions, so that total sizes the selected cohort; it does not measure sponsor equity, current value, or investment returns. The audit follows control and ownership events instead.

sections.title: Transaction value does not measure sponsor return
paragraphs: The cohort total combines mixed company-reported headline transaction values. Some announcements use enterprise value, some use equity value, and others use another headline convention. The total is useful for sizing the selected cohort, but it is not a common-basis valuation series.
Record transaction size, control at the cutoff, ownership events, and fund return separately. A reported deal value cannot fill the missing fields.

sections.title: Liquidity can leave sponsor control intact
paragraphs: The cohort generated IPO proceeds, partial stake sales, refinancings, dividend distributions, continuation transactions, and creditor-led ownership changes. Those events matter, but they are not interchangeable. Under the stated definition, a clean realization requires a completed sale, broad public distribution, or equivalent transfer that removes the original sponsor group’s control.

The finding concerns an inventory of control investments assembled during the low-rate software take-private boom. Conventional exits remained unresolved at the cutoff, even where an “IPO,” “liquidity event,” or reported “exit” had occurred. Those labels alone do not establish that sponsor control ended.

sections.title: Classify the event before counting an exit
paragraphs: Full sponsor realization sits at the top of the hierarchy. Partial liquidity records proceeds while control continues. Creditor transfers remain separate because a lender-led ownership change can extinguish sponsor control without creating sponsor proceeds. Continuing sponsor ownership applies when no higher-priority classification is supported.

SailPoint shows how the definition changes the count. Its listing created a market price and a route to sell down, but continuing sponsor voting control kept the IPO outside the completed-control-exit category.
bullets: Current-control evidence takes precedence over transaction labels.
An IPO is not automatically a full realization.
A continuation transaction may create liquidity while preserving effective control.
A creditor transfer is not evidence of sponsor proceeds.

sections.title: A cutoff cannot settle the eventual outcome
paragraphs: A zero-realization count at this cutoff is not evidence that zero future realizations will occur. Most acquisitions were only three to five years into sponsor ownership, while technology holding periods at exit had lengthened to roughly five years by the end of 2025.

Strategic sales, sponsor-to-sponsor deals, public sell-downs, continuation structures, recapitalizations, and operational improvement remained possible. The record supports delayed realization and fragmented ownership outcomes, not permanent impairment of the entire cohort.

sections.title: The missing cash flows prevent a return calculation
paragraphs: A cohort MOIC or IRR would require sponsor equity contributions, acquisition debt, add-on investment, operating cash retained or distributed, dividend proceeds, partial-sale proceeds, continuation-vehicle pricing, management dilution, fees, fund allocations, and current marks. Those fields are not available in the public package at the level required for a return calculation.

The package supports the stated control map and event inventory, but omits the underlying transaction source ledger. Readers therefore cannot reproduce every row from primary filings using this site alone. That limitation applies even when the classifications appear plausible.
bullets: Do not compare current enterprise value with announced purchase price as a synthetic return.
Do not treat every IPO or partial sale as a full exit.
Do not infer sponsor loss from creditor stress without reconstructing prior cash flows.
